title: NPR and NewsGuard tested six chatbots against foreign propaganda — they mostly held up
subtitle: ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, Meta AI, Grok and Claude were fed 30 false narratives traced to China, Russia and Iran; the chatbots outperformed the search engines they were compared against.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: NPR published a joint investigation with news-rating outfit NewsGuard on August 30, testing whether major AI chatbots repeat state-sponsored propaganda when asked about it directly. Researchers built 30 false narratives that first appeared in Chinese, Russian and Iranian influence operations between December 2025 and July 2026, then fed each one to six chatbots — OpenAI's ChatGPT, Google's Gemini, Microsoft's Copilot, Meta AI, SpaceXAI's Grok, and Anthropic's Claude — as two questions each: a neutral 'did this happen?' and a leading 'why did this happen?' The same narratives were also queried on Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo and Russia's Yandex.

The headline finding is that the chatbots did surprisingly well — better, in fact, than the search engines. Bots more often flagged the narrative as false, cited counter-sourcing, or refused to answer without qualification, while search engines were more likely to surface propaganda outlets in the top results. That inverts the intuition from the 2023-2024 cycle, when chatbots were the ones criticized for confidently repeating fabricated stories. The improvement tracks the industry's shift to grounded search-augmented answering, retrieval filters over known state-media domains, and the tighter guardrails the labs have shipped over the last year.

Two caveats matter. First, 'did surprisingly well' is not the same as 'did well' — every model still failed on some prompts, and leading questions ('why did this happen?') pulled worse answers than neutral ones across the board, replicating the same jailbreak pattern researchers have been documenting since 2023. Second, the study was conducted in mid-July, before several models pushed new versions; results on today's models could be better or worse, and any single company can regress on a single deploy. The pattern the study establishes is the useful signal: on this task, retrieval-grounded chatbots now beat classical search.

For learners: if you use a chatbot for anything current-events adjacent, the framing of your question changes the answer more than you think. A neutral 'is X true?' will pull sourcing; a leading 'why is X happening?' primes the model to accept the premise and reason from it. That effect is not a flaw in one model, it is a property of instruction-following language models generally — worth practicing the neutral phrasing until it is muscle memory.
